narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 51% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped just above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking in the third year of law school was the strongest influence, and it pushed the prediction toward failure. Placing in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) is substantially lower than the average of roughly 6 among students who were accepted. Your first-year ranking in the bottom decile (compared to an average of 6 for accepted students) also pulled the prediction in the same direction, though less strongly.

Your family income bracket worked in the opposite direction. Being in the Low income group actually made the model slightly more optimistic about your chances, because very few students from that bracket appear in the data and those who do sometimes outperform expectations. However, this positive effect was not large enough to overcome the impact of your two low class rankings.

Taken together, the model concluded your academic performance signals a higher risk of failing the bar exam than the school is willing to accept.

What you should do next is straightforward: focus on improving your class rank in the remaining years, seek targeted bar-prep support early, and consider reapplying once you have stronger upper-year grades. Many students in similar situations have succeeded by addressing exactly these performance gaps. (248 words)
